Messages.Body:
Folks:

More and more it seems to me that Immortal Grapple is a broken card.
That is, it has three characteristics that allow it to dominate any
Methusaleh-to-Methusaleh interaction: difficult to prevent,
disproportionate results, extremely wide applicability.

First, it is nearly impossible to counter. Yes, the antidote to IG is
the lowly maneuver. The problem is the the antidote can be rather
easily countered itself. For example, the Brujah are usually packing
CEL, which has 4 maneuver cards (at least). Or, the tidy IG user can
always include Fake Out. Moreover, the rush cards carry their own
maneuver. In other words, maneuvers often don't help against IG.

Second, IG almost always produces disproportional results, that is I
have seen 4-cap vampires completely burn fully-blooded 8- and 9-cap
vampires.

Third, IG will work again nearly any combat defense deck.

In my (admittedly limited) experience, the Methusaleh with a Potence
Rush deck will almost always utterly destroy his/her prey. Now, I'm
sure that many of you will reply that the Rush Potence deck (a) has
trouble actually ousting his/her prey, and (b) often runs out of cards.
Well, folks, that is cold cold consolation to the prey who has been
savaged by this broken card.

When I first started dropping by this forum, folks were griping about
S:CE. Hey, I'd much much rather face S:CE, which of course is
primarily defensive, that sit downwind from Rush Potence.

Your thoughts?
Madman

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Madman wrote:
>>More and more it seems to me that Immortal Grapple is a broken card.
That is, it has three characteristics that allow it to dominate any
Methusaleh-to-Methusaleh interaction: difficult to prevent,
disproportionate results, extremely wide applicability.>>

Yes, Immortal Grapple is a powerful card when viewed as an independant
component. The problem is, however, that, within a context, decks that use
Immortal Grapple are simply not any more effective than any other deck type. As
such, yes, IG decks are pretty much the be all and end all of combat, but these
decks are not disproportionally effective, when compared to other (non combat)
deck types.

>>First, it is nearly impossible to counter. Yes, the antidote to IG is
the lowly maneuver. The problem is the the antidote can be rather
easily countered itself.>>

Again, you need to look at the card in context. Yes, the Brujah have access to
Cel and plenty of manuvers, but IG Rush decks are *incredibly* card
intensive--a given combat can burn through 6-10 cards easily. As a result, such
decks need to be very tight, and don't have room for cards that jam your hand
or are only conditionally useful. Trying to fit all of the neccessary combat
cards into a 90 card deck (Bum's Rush, Torn Signpost, Undead Strength, Immortal
Grapple, Taste of Vitae--that is half the deck right there...) is difficult,
and when you have to make room for copious manuvers, you run out of room for
other stuff you need. As a result, manuvers are often fairly low on the list of
"Must make room for" cards. If you have too many, they jam up your hand when
your opponents don't have manuvers. If you don't have enough, your opponents
will invariably have more manuvers than you.

>>For example, the Brujah are usually packing
CEL, which has 4 maneuver cards (at least).>>

They don't need 4. They only need Flash, which is an incredibly powerful card.
Still, you are unlikely to run into more than 8 Flashes in a generic, effective
Rush deck. There simply isn't room for any more.

>>Or, the tidy IG user can always include Fake Out.>>

The lack of card cycling on Fake Out is a sever disadvantage for a Rush deck.

>>Moreover, the rush cards carry their own maneuver.>>

Block them. Pull out a Zip Gun. Play a couple of manuvers. Wave.

>>In other words, maneuvers often don't help against IG.>>

I assure you that this is incorrect. Yeah, a half assed inclusion of 4 or 5
Fake Outs isn't going to get you anywhere, but if you are *really* concerned
about an IG Rush deck, including 10-12 disciplined manuvers and a bunch of Zip
Guns will slow down the Rush deck enough for it to get killed before it kills
you.

>>Second, IG almost always produces disproportional results, that is I
have seen 4-cap vampires completely burn fully-blooded 8- and 9-cap
vampires.>>

Yes. Again, Rush decks need to be able to do this, otherwise they would not be
viable decks. Also again, Rush decks are simply not more effective (in terms of
game victory) than compareable Bleed or Vote decks.

>>Third, IG will work again nearly any combat defense deck.>>

Fortitude/Protean shuts down IG right quick. Obediance shuts down IG right
quick. Strong manuver shuts down IG right quick.

>>In my (admittedly limited) experience, the Methusaleh with a Potence
Rush deck will almost always utterly destroy his/her prey.>>

Any deck that can't defend itself against its predator will be utterly
destroyed. If you are a S+B deck,and I have no S+B defense (no deflections, no
Rush), you will utterly destroy me. If you are a vote deck, and I have no vote
defense (no intercept, no Rush) you will utterly destroy me. Yes, when a Rush
deck has, as its prey, a deck that has no viable combat defense, it will
destroy it. That is what happens when you have no defenses against your
predator. On the other hand, having a good supply of combat defense means that
the IG Rush deck will be slowed down, and likely ousted before it kills you
outright.

>>Now, I'm sure that many of you will reply that the Rush Potence deck (a) has
trouble actually ousting his/her prey, and (b) often runs out of cards.
Well, folks, that is cold cold consolation to the prey who has been
savaged by this broken card.>>

It has nothing to do with cold consolation. It is part of the reason that such
decks aren't completely dominating. They are hard to build. They are hard to
play. As a result, you don't run into them that often. Because people don't run
into them that often, people don't consider them when building their decks. You
always say "hey--how is this deck going to survive against a S+B deck?" and not
think twice about including 8 Wakes and 8 Deflections. If those 16 cards were
viable IG defense instead (Obediance/Manuver), you would not be as vulnerable
to an IG deck. it takes very little to unbalance a Rush deck, and result in in
getting ousted instead of it killing you.

The problem is that there is never enough room in a deck to include all the
defenses you want. Usually, combat defense is on the low end of the "need"
list, so it doesn't show up. This is what makes Rush decks go--people not
including the needed defenses.

Having been playing this sort of deck for years in tournament and non
tournament play, I assure you that if people play with viable combat defense
(Fortitude, manuvers, Obediance, Elisium), Rush decks are very difficult to
actually win with. On the other hand, when you sit down at a game with people
who have no combat defense, the Rush deck eats them alive.

>>When I first started dropping by this forum, folks were griping about
S:CE. Hey, I'd much much rather face S:CE, which of course is
primarily defensive, that sit downwind from Rush Potence.>>

Play a Ventrue deck with 20% combat defense--10 Skin of Steel/8 Majesty. Throw
in an Elisium or two. Your Rush predator will be slowed down enough that either
you will oust your prey or the Rush deck will be ousted before you are.

You just need to view combat defense as an important aspect of your deck if you
expect to see a Rush deck. The Rush deck doesn't need to be shut down. It just
needs to be unbalanced.

I play a very effective IG Rush deck. It has won tournaments. It wins games on
a regular basis. It is a competetive deck, but not overly powerful by any
stretch of the imagination. It only has, however, 8 manuvers (from Behind You!)
plus the 12 Bum's Rush manuvers. It'll rarely have access to more than 2
manuvers per combat--you have a gun and a manuver card, you are at long range,
and my action is wasted, which is very bad for such a deck. Most of the
vampires are small (5 or less), so Obediance is usually a very effective
defense. Again, a wasted action. Enough wasted actions, and the Rush deck gets
killed. Yes, my deck has won a few tournaments, but it has not won far more
than it has.

I question "wide applicability". You must have a vamp with Potence,
and you must be using some sort of effective hand strikes. These are
either: more Potence, or aggravated hand damage. pot/PRO is a nasty
thing to do to people, but difficult to pull off. POT/POT/POT is
somewhat easier to pull off, but to guarantee its effectiveness needs
to be filed in a POT Rush deck, which has its own problems.

>First, it is nearly impossible to counter. Yes, the antidote to IG is

A deck which can consistently outmaneuver and Grapple you cannot do
anything else, often not even beat you up once it has hold of you.

>the lowly maneuver. The problem is the the antidote can be rather

>easily countered itself. For example, the Brujah are usually packing
>CEL, which has 4 maneuver cards (at least). Or, the tidy IG user can
>always include Fake Out. Moreover, the rush cards carry their own
>maneuver. In other words, maneuvers often don't help against IG.

Fake Out makes me want to hurl. Effective? Yes. Hand-clogging,
especially since one is often one card down from a Bum's Rush? Yes.
Probably not worth putting in your deck? Yes. (There is a contingent
pondering whether Trap is better as an anti-run-away card. It might
well be.)

>Third, IG will work again nearly any combat defense deck.

For. Ti. Tude. I submit that FOR cards and S:CE are the two most used
forms of combat defense, with Dodge coming in a distant third. IG
will not do squat against superior Fortitude.

>In my (admittedly limited) experience, the Methusaleh with a Potence

>Rush deck will almost always utterly destroy his/her prey. Now, I'm

>sure that many of you will reply that the Rush Potence deck (a) has
>trouble actually ousting his/her prey, and (b) often runs out of cards.
> Well, folks, that is cold cold consolation to the prey who has been
>savaged by this broken card.

There are a number of decks which have trouble doing anything other
than hosing their predator and/or prey. It's quite easy to build such
a deck - an ill-built intercept deck also produces such results (often
hosing BOTH predator and prey while totally failing to oust anyone).
Should we consider Auspex broken?

Potence Rush can actually hold its own in the hands of a skilled
player. Sure, it has trouble competing with weenie presence
misdirection/bleed for speed, but it also provides an enormous Fear
Factor for those weenie decks by its very existence, since a weenie
deck sitting next to POT Rush is basically going to be ousted early.

>When I first started dropping by this forum, folks were griping about
>S:CE. Hey, I'd much much rather face S:CE, which of course is
>primarily defensive, that sit downwind from Rush Potence.

Would you? The Ventrue block your bleed, Majesty, and untap so they
can optionally deflect the next one. Or, on offence, they bleed you,
Majesty, untap, and call a damage vote. Either way you're screwed
just as much as having all your vampires torched by an IG deck.
Probably more, since you always have the option of not bringing out
vampires (targets), but you don't have the option of not making your
pool available to be voted or bled.

-- Derek

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Sorrow wrote:
>>Excuse me? So now we are making the determination on how broken a
card is based on how well the decks that use it do? What about Thoughts
Betrayed. The combat decks that utilized that card didn't really win a
disporportionate number of games but that didn't stop people from bitching
and moaning about how broken it was.>>

I'm not determining whether anything is broken. I am pointing out that IG is a
powerful card, but the effect it has on the environment is not greater than it
should be. Without IG, combat, as a strategy, is impossible to succeed with.
With IG, combat is a viable, but not overly powerful strategy.

Many found TB to be outside of the spirit of the original game paradigm. Thus,
it was changed.

>>Who cares. We are talking about what happens when your vamps are IG'd
and now it's not really all that easy to get away from unless you yourself
are playing a combat deck that can get away.>>

I claim that this is not the case.

>>Not that difficult. I've built a lot of Cel/Pot decks and it's not often
when I don't have the right card in my hand when I need it.>>

If you have too many of too different cards, you don't get the ones you need
when you need them.

>>Uhh, there are alot of maneuver cards that have multi-purposes that make it
much easier for you...>>

These cards all require superior CEL to do something other than manuver. If you
are building a deck that is going to have enough CEL to make use of these
multi-purpose cards, you are either using large vampires (which will get you
killed) or *lots* of Celerity skill cards, which you don't have room for. A
Rush deck *needs* POT. If it has to have CEL too, it just isn't getting
anywhere.

>>All you need are those multi-purpose cards.>>

And the CEL to make it work. I assure you, you aren't going to make a viable
Rush deck that will consistiently have POT and CEL.

>>I find it rare that a deck that isn't a combat deck pack maneuvers.>>

Yes--that is why the IG decks kill them. If they did pack manuvers, the IG
decks wouldn't kill them. Do you find it rare that a deck that isn't a bleed
deck packs bleed bounce?

>>And even if they do, it's not all that many. So all you need is just 1 (2 at
max,
generally) to get back within range. And once you are there, the other vamp is
usually screwed.>>

Yup. If you are worried about IG, you use manuvers. If you are worried about
S+B, you add bleed bounce. If you are worried about votes, you add intercept.
Every strategy has a foil.

>>What about Pursuit, which also doubles up as an Additional Strike?>>

At CEL. Relying on CEL in a Rush deck is fruitless.

>>It doesn't matter. Again, since when is it that the determination on how
broken a card is is dependant on how well the deck does that is based on it?
It is
a given that a Rush deck has a difficult time winning games. This fact was
pointed out by the original poster. But it doesn't make much of a difference
for
that deck's prey (or sometimes predator). Once a vamp is IG'd, there is *very,
very* little it can do to defend itself if it too isn't a close quarters combat
deck.>>

Or is using Fortitude. Or is using Obediance to avoid combat all together. Or
has manuvers to not get caught.

>>Again, it is very rare that a non-combat deck uses Zip Gun and copious
maneuvers of it's own...>>

Only because they don't want to be able to defend themselves against IG. If you
are worried about IG combat, you include defenses against it, much like you
include bleed defenses if you are worried about S+B.

>>Ok, and then *you* have hand jam when you aren't facing a Rush deck.
Great trade off...>>

If you are using Deflections, and your opponent never bleeds you, then *they*
jam your hand. Every defense needs to be weighed against the likelyhood of you
needing it. Just because Rush decks aren't that common doesn't mean you
shouldn't need to have to weigh the cost of defense against them.

>>So. TB decks weren't all that more effective (in terms of game victory)...>>

Again, the problem with TB was that it removed too much of the game from play.

>>They are hard to play and win with. They are not hard to play to be able to
decimate vamps.>>

They are if their opponents have defenses. If your opponents can't defend
themselves against whatever strategy you are using, you will decimate them,
regardless of the strategy you are using.

>>So. That doesn't lessen the overall effect that IG has on the environment.>>

Correct. The effect that IG has on the environment is that it makes combat a
viable strategy. Without it, combat would be unplayable, as combat defense is
simply too effective and too easy, compared to the amount of work it takes to
make a combat deck work.

>>People down here run into them all the time. Sometimes what they add helps,
most often it doesn't.>>

If they run into them all the time, they should be able to make very effective
anti-combat decks, and not have to worry about the opportunity cost of the
defenses. If you are playing against a lot of combat decks, make a deck with 18
Flashes in it. You will shut them down.

>>Exactly. So who is going to put in a crap load of maneuvers and sacrifice
their defenses for the other archetypes? Or sacrifice their offensive
power?>>

The people who want to not get killed by IG decks. If you change the question
to "Who is going to put in a crap load of deflections?" because of rampant S+B,
no one is going to think twice about doing so.

>>Not true. Defenses show up down here. Generally, it's not enough.>>

Then use more.

>>This is *not* the issue and I do not understand why you keep bringing it
up.>>

Apparently 'cause I thought to myself "Hmm. How can I most irritate Sorrow." as
I was writing my post.

>>Who cares if the deck is difficult or not to win with. The point that is
being made is that the _one_ card, Immortal Grapple, is overly powerful.>>

As it is easily countered by common defenses--manuvers, Obediance, Fortitude,
aggro hand strikes, it is hard to agree that it is overly powerful.

>>Again, this deals with winning with the deck. The only thing that is going

you think - a simple Aid from Bats worked fine for me in a recent
tournament (an IG deck was my prey, and I repeatedly intercepted him

thing well - beat up vampires. They bleed for 1 per vamp, making them
a risky proposition to win with. Using your example, a Thoughts
Betrayed deck bled for a LOT more than 1 per vamp, and also called

that same deck and you would contest vampires.

>much easier for you...

nuts when you didn't happen to have a CEL vampire handy.

>All you need are those multi-purpose cards.

You mean Pursuit? What other "those" are you thinking of? I look
through Celerity, and I discover that there are only three cards which

>I find it rare that a deck that isn't a combat deck pack maneuvers. And

>

>> They don't need 4. They only need Flash, which is an incredibly powerful

>

What about Flash, which also provides a press for those pesky times
when someone outmaneuvers you? Since you're talking about a CEL
vampire here (or Pursuit is worthless), you can play a Flash to try to
catch someone, they use a Fake Out and Zip Gun to get away. You
press, from that SAME FLASH card. They are out of maneuvers and you

The definition of "broken", for me, is "provides a game imbalance that
can be exploited to significant advantage for the player". Thoughts
Betrayed was like this. Return to Innocence was like this. Pulled
Fangs was like this. Fame was like this. Majesty is STILL like this,
and is only kept in check slightly by Immortal Grapple.

Immortal Grapple is NOT LIKE THIS. I have difficulty even saying that
it provides a game imbalance, but I absolutely, totally object to the
thought that IG can be exploited to *SIGNIFICANT* advantage for the
IG-deck player. You can vaporize all your prey's vampires and all
your predator's vampires with an IG deck and accomplish nothing but
get all three of you ousted by your grand-predator's Hideous Weenie
Horde. NOWHERE is anyone afraid of an IG deck coming in and "sweeping
a tournament again". But they sure as hell were afraid of the RtI and
Thoughts Betrayed decks... and the Hostile Takeover decks are still
pretty damn mean.

>prey (or sometimes predator). Once a vamp is IG'd, there is *very, very*
>little

Fortitude, fortitude, fortitude, fortitude. Or, if you've got
Protean, poke their eye out.

>
>Again, it is very rare that a non-combat deck uses Zip Gun and copious

long range than take 7 at close. It's very simple - block the Rush,

What's the difference between being blocked by a vampire and trading
punches for 1 at close range, and between being blocked by a vampire,
pulling out a Zip Gun, and shooting him for 1 at long range?

range combat, if you want to beat the hell out of people but don't
want to be IG'd. The deck I mentioned above used Aid from Bats,
Carrion Crows, and a couple Murder of Crows to hand out 3-5 points of
damage at range per round. Aid from Bats provides a convenient press,
so I didn't have much trouble killing people who didn't S:CE (dodge
being worthless against CC and MoC).

>> It has nothing to do with cold consolation. It is part of the reason that

See above. What other criteria would you use to determine how broken
a card is? I could point out that Rotshit is pretty broken, taken as
ONLY a card - it defeats almost EVERYTHING, including Fortitude, IG,
Majesty, etc... But is Rotshit broken? No, because there's no way to
exploit it more effectively than anything else. Legbiter's Rotshit
decks are functional, but not over-powerful, since it can only pull

If you want to build one that has a hope of winning, they are hard to
build.

>

Well, I can play an intercept deck and totally screw my predator until

the Tzimisce be removed from the set?

What overall effect? People either include maneuvers and IG has a
hard go of it, or they include Majesties and die miserably like the
presence-bleeders they are.

it, or they include intercept and the Malks run over them like a
week-old possum.

>power?

Someone who doesn't want to die if they happen to sit next to a combat
deck? My PRO/dom deck has room for either 7 Delaying Tactics, or 7
Quick Melds. I flipped a coin before playing it in the tournament,
because I knew I could either shut down votes *OR* combat. The coin
said "DT", so I put the DTs in and sure nuff, there was ONE vote deck
out of 18 players. There were, unfortunately for me, five Potence
combat decks. I now consider maneuvers much higher on the list of

Zip Guns, eh?

someone else that way? I personally believe that most players build a
deck with the intent that it win, ie. gain victory points. Someone
who plays an IG deck well will do well. Someone who plays an IG deck
poorly will do poorly. Someone who plays a Ventrue vote deck poorly

See above. A powerful card isn't worth crap if you can't find a way
to use it to win with. How about Shadow of the Beast? Protean, costs
1 blood. Card text: "Put this card on the acting vampire. The
vampire with this card gets one optional maneuver each combat. A
vampire may have only one Shadow of the Beast. (S) As above, and this

powerful card. But is it broken? No? Why not? It gives a vampire a
built-in Flash -every- combat. It can't be removed - at ALL. It can

damage? ... But the fact of the matter is, it's NOT broken, for

consistently gain VPs.

>help that Ventrue deck is the Elysium. Yes, the SoS is going to make it so

Um, the Skin of Steels are going to run the Rush deck out of offensive

Majesty unless he wastes another IG - and most Rush decks don't

>that the
>vamps don't take damage, but they still can only hit with hands due to the
>IG. Can
>they use those Majesties? Nope.

Sure, they can - use 'em on the OTHER guy they're sitting next to, who
probably isn't playing IG Rush.

>First, it is nearly impossible to counter. Yes, the antidote to IG is

This is true of many deck types. I can puts lots of intercept into a
deck to stop bleed actions, but you can just as easily put more stealth
in.

In almost all situations in Jyhad, the game revolves around a subtle
"Activity, Counter-Activity, Counter-Counter Activity" interplay. e.g.

Activity: Bleeding
C-A: Block
C-C-A: Stealth
C-C-C-A: Intercept
C-C-C-C-A: Unblockability
C-C-C-C-C-A: Bleed Reduction
C-C-C-C-C-C-A: Increase the bleed
C-C-C-C-C-C-C-A:Bounce the bleed

And so on. Now, that isn't necessarily the best route, or the most
productive route, but it's a possible route.

>
>Second, IG almost always produces disproportional results, that is I
>have seen 4-cap vampires completely burn fully-blooded 8- and 9-cap
>vampires.

Yes. This is intentional. Look at Wolf Claws. With it, Igo the Hungry
(1 capacity) can torporise Arika (11 capacity).

Again, move back to another activity in the game. Gloria Giovanni (the
smallest vampire with DOM) is 4 capacity, but for an investment of 4
pool, you can make a person lose 7 pool in one simple action - Govern
the Unaligned, Command (+1 bleed, no restrictions), Conditioning.

Also, consider the fact that it isn't the IG /per se/ that is causing
the disproportionate results, it's IG backed up with lots of other
things. Again, that's true elsewhere. The reason why many people
objected to RtoI was the ability to cause massive pool loss very, very
quickly, without the investment in time and cards in your deck.

>
>Third, IG will work again nearly any combat defense deck.

Many commonly used defences, perhaps. If that's the problem, though,
there are many other combat defences that *will* work, in the right
circumstances. Note, this may or may not be "enough" other defences,
but there are other defences. Also, I know that some of these are very,
very uncommon things to happen, but they are possible. Other cards are
very common, though - or *could* be. This is unlike the RtoI situation
where there were very few defences that could be enacted, and were often
quite specific. There are many specific defences here, but also generic
ones, too. Some are also very slow, but if the rush deck isn't your
predator or prey, you may well have enough time to cope with that.

So, a (no doubt incomplete) of things to do in combat to save your skin,
or get theirs:

- Elysium: The Arboretum
- 1 maneuver, Terror Frenzy
- Shadow Step
- Quick Meld (outpaces a Brujah deck for maneuvers, no questions)
- Cailean
- Leather Jacket
- Flak Jacket/Resplendent Protector
- Mariel, Lady Thunder
- Fortitude Damage Prevention
- Chimerstry Damage Prevention
- Living Manse
- Legacy of Power
- Phobia
- Illusions of the Kindred
- Brujah Frenzy (send an unblocked rush elsewhere, Brujah very common)
- Rotschreck (can prevent the burn versus, say, pot/pro)
- Thoughts Betrayed (if, say, UndStr is the problem, not Torn Signpost)
- Fake Out (blocking takes the rush maneuver away, and you will draw
their maneuvers)
- Maneuver granters - IR Goggles, Shadow of the Beast, Patagia
- Ghoul Retainer + Weapon
- Undead Persistence (for "do not enter torpor" effect)
- Obedience (esp. in your 3 or 4 versus an 8 or 9 situation)
- Mind of a Child (prevents the use of potence, they have no stealth)
- Erosion (every little helps)
- Song of Serenity
- Carrion Crows
- Damage dealing retainers
- Play Gangrel, and do something like Lucky Blow + Claws (little damage
prevention available in many pot/cel decks)
- Flesh of Marble
- Secure Haven

And so on. Don't forget that there are other ways to screw over a
weenie potence/celerity deck, too. Maybe bring out a vampire *fast* and
call Masquerade Enforcement, so that they have to spend more on vampires
etc.

And another important consideration is that you don't have to protect
every single vampire you have. Sometimes, you will have to let one go.
However, if you can keep that one vampire alive who will give you the
bleed for the oust, or the votes for the KRC, or whatever, it can be
worth just defending that one.

>>Again I contend that it is not that difficult.>>

Coming from a guy who has played, pretty much exclusively, an IG Rush combat
deck in tournaments for the last 4 years, I assure you that the balance between
manuvers and not manuvers in a Rush deck is a very teniuous balance. Yes, you
can have lots of manuvers, but then they jam your hand and you have less of the

Ok. For example, my Rush deck plays 12 Bum's Rush and 8 Behind You. In my
environment, everyone is very warry of combat, so lots of manuvers as a defense
isn't unusual. A deck that is prefectly viable on its own can include 12 or so

and destabilize it.

to cause damage) is seriously watering down itself.>>

But it isn't getting killed by the IG deck, which is what you wanted in the
first place. All defenses water down a deck. That is part of the game--that you
need to weigh the cost of defense vs offense. Again, I mantain that it isn't
unusual for a deck to have, say, 8 Wakes and 8 Deflections (in fact, my current
DOM deck has 9 of each). This is 20% bleed defense. No one blinks twice at this
sort of inclusion, and no one will complain that it waters down your deck--it
is just inherrently acceptable in terms of deck design. 20% bleed defense,
because you are worried about bleed decks. Why, if you are worried about Rush
decks, is it then a bad idea to include 20% combat defense?

it, all it says is that (paraphrase) all but hand strikes are denied. So
regardless of what kind of combat cards you have, once you are IG'd, it's
effect is
still occuring.>>

Right. IG keeps you from using anything but hand strikes. If you don't care
about anything but hand strikes (because you are either a hand to hand combat
deck, or only concerned with combat defense), then the effect of the card is to
allow your opponent to kill you. If you have Fortitude, you deny your opponent
the ability to kill you.

>>Does not matter. I'm not sure how many more times I have to say this.>>

Please, please say it more.

>>Once you are IG'd, you *cannot play any cards* that are not hand strikes/
hand damage.>>

Thus you need to avoid being IGed if you want to play such cards. If you don't,
you don't care if you are IGed. If you are using Fortitude, you don't care if
you are IGed. If you are using S:CE, then you do, so you would be better off
avoiding the IG in the first place.

>>Compare IG to TB which basically does the same thing, but at the cost
of 2 blood. The only thing that TB does above and beyond IG is that it
doesn't allow you to play strike cards even if they are hand strikes/hand
damage.>>

Yes. The cards are roughly comparable at this point. It costs 2 blood and DOM,
as it is in, essentially, a non combat discipline.

>>Fortitude still effectively counters it (in that your vamp doesn't

die; an argument that you seem to think has any bearing on the overall
effectiveness of a card),>>

It does. People keep saying IG has no counters. It has plenty--avoidance
through Manuvers/Obediance/Elisium/etc or damage prevention, which stops what
IG allows. IG, in and of itself, isn't going to kill anyone--if I play IG and
then hit you for 1, what good is that going to do?

>>you can still Wolf's Claws/Bone Spur/Etc. still work when it's played, yadda,

yadda. So for what it does v. what it costs, especially when compared to other
cards with similar effect, yes, IG is overpowered (or broken, depending on your
view).>>

I don't really see how you establish this point, but you are welcome to. TB is
now a perfeclty balanced card. Compared to IG, they have very similar effects.
TB costs more than IG, as TB comes from DOM, a non combat discipline (a
precident set by other cards that provide out of discipline effects, like
Behind You and Cat Burgulary). If TB is acceptable (with the appropriate
errata), and IG has a similar effect for a comparable cost (taking the
discipline factor into acount), then ergo, IG is a balanced card.

>You play TB on an IG deck, and they're more than likely screwed. Well,
>in my group they would be.

It all depends on how you play them. If the deck would revolve around,
as one of mine would, Increased Strength and Undead Strength, yes, they
would be. However, were I to have access to the cards needed, you can
play Torn Signpost and Fists of Death - 5 damage on a POT vampire -
neither of which are strike cards. Follow up with Disarm and Decapitate
as necessary.

Similar things happen with several combat styles:

- cel/pot can play Torn Signpost, Fists of Death, Taste of Vitae and
Blur, and still IG you
- obf/pot can play similar to above, though it might struggle to deal as
much damage
- ani/for can play DotB and Skin of Steel, getting you at the end of the
round
- tha/for has the Weather Control/Dawn Op combo to try out for size
- ani/pro can always attempt to use Carrion Crows and Claws. Your TB
will knock out the Scorpion Sting, however, but then you need to
be playing celerity to really capitalise on dodges and blurs
- weapon/cel never plays strike cards - ammo cards and blurs are still
playable, and if you want Obf/Cel, play Disguised Weapon too
- +HD/cel (opt) can have increased hand damage to start with (either
from vampires innate ability, or library cards) and then blur

And so on. These are all ways decks *can* be played if they view TB as
a threat - more annoying and difficult to play, perhaps, but playable.

TB is still a good card - it can, as you say, nullify some decks - but
it's no longer quite so powerful. The major people who would, IMO, have
more of a problem getting around TB are the Assamites, unfortunately.

Hmm.... a couple of AUS weenies to get you the intercept to start with
(and Eagle's Sight).

Zoe would work well, with AUS obf cel.
Isabel de Leon with AUS (and no hunting restriction).
Dorian Strack with AUS cel.

Then play with Mages on Speed. Use aus (inferior is all that's needed,
unless you come up against a lot of damage prevention and want to press)
to Fast Reaction. A few Thefts probably wouldn't go amiss, especially
if you're short on Taste. Shotgun Ritual allows you to get to the
"nice" strikes - Cauldron of Blood and Walk of Flame are still by far
the best second round Thaumaturgy strikes, for my money. And use cel to
capitalise on it with a blur (or other form of additional strikes).

You have a few nice vampires at your disposal for this:

Ian Forestal has AUS THA cel (effectively)
Thomas Thorne has aus cel tha (but he's smaller than most)
Al Ashrad has THA CEL aus (a superb arrangement for this)
Parnassus has CEL aus tha (and with CEL, he can do multiple smaller tha
strikes)
Javier Montoya has THA AUS cel (and if you plan to use Fame in such a
deck, his rescue ability might be wanted)
Klaus van der Veken has CEL aus tha (as Parnassus, and 2 votes)
Ethan Locke has THA aus cel (2 votes, too)

There are other vampires with all three disciplines (e.g. Gwendolyn,
Lucian) but these are the ones who initially make me think "Could be
useful". Obviously, if you're using bigger vampires for the kill,
you'll need a couple of Wakes (of whatever form) such that you can use
each vampire multiple times during the same turn, or have them take
actions during your minion phase.
